//rope: Cable texture. BuildHalfCable flat-samples ONE point of it, because CubeMeshUtil scales UVs by the axis scale and anything leaving [0,1] samples the neighbouring atlas sprite - that was the striping. See docs/KNOWN-ISSUES.md. Keep comments OUT of "textures": every key there is parsed as a CompositeTexture.
//nopower: A PLAIN tower is not a mechanical power node and cannot become one: it has no intake cell, so it drives nothing whatever stands beside it. The intake is cell [3,0,0] of a ropeway:drivestation, which is a different footing block with the same fifteen offsets - see drivestation.json. A trial build put the hookup on the bullwheel four blocks up here, and it was abandoned: getting an axle into the air cost about sixteen vanilla blocks of scaffold, and the run had to cross the cells the cabin hanger flies through. The intake sits at the FOOT of a station's machine leg instead. Do not move it back onto a crossarm cell. See docs/POWER-AND-STORAGE.md.
//metal: NOT this footing's own decoration. `metal` is the STATION RAIL and the outrigger plates, which BEPylonBase.OnTesselation draws in C# off textures["metal"] (BEPylonBase.cs:603) and flat-samples like the cable - Array.Fill(mesh.Uv, 0.5f) at :989 - so only this sprite's CENTRE texel is ever seen and it must stay in the plate/ family, whose centre is within 1 L of its own mean. riveted/iron1 fails that by 6.5 L. It is plate/IRON and not the plate/steel `shaft` wears, which is a SECOND rule and a rendered one: SpanMath.TrimForTowers draws eight blocks of 2.2x4-unit bar at every tower on every line, so this is the longest continuous geometry the mod has, and steel's flat sample of 126.5 L made it the brightest object on a tower - 37% brighter than the crossarm it hangs under, with the haul cable a thread beside it (renders/palette/zoom-rail.png). plate/iron flat-samples 95.0: one step UNDER `shaft`, 2.5 L off the riveted crossarm's own mean, still 21 L clear of the rope, and it reads as a bar rather than a highlight. The footing's own plate and boss are on `shaft` instead, so a cosmetic edit to the footing cannot silently repaint every rail on every line. A key no shape face uses still bakes into the atlas (Block.cs:2514); `rope` here has always worked that way.

attributes.//maxLineLength: 320 = 10 chunks, and it MITIGATES the truncated-line failure class rather than closing it (docs/KNOWN-ISSUES.md R1-R4). This used to say a line shorter than the server's MaxChunkRadius can never have a tower unload while a rider is anywhere on it. MaxChunkRadius 12, i.e. 384 blocks (ServerConfig.cs:925), is a CAP on the loaded radius and not the radius: ServerMain.GetAllowedChunkRadius is min(MaxChunkRadius, ceil(Viewdistance/32)), and the shipped client default of 256 makes that 8 chunks = 256 blocks - so a full-length line outruns the window by 64 and a player at one END of one has the far end dark. What 320 does buy is that the MIDDLE of a full-length line holds all of it, and that most lines are well under 256 end to end. Raising this back toward 512 makes both worse. It also carries the POWER design: the cabin runs at the live speed of the drives on its line (BEPylonBase.DriveSpeedOn), which is only honest while all of them are loaded - the same radius argument doing a second job, with the same caveat, which is why EntityRopewayCabin.MayStart refuses only on a chain that is not truncated. Where the old design wrote 'the cabin must never read live network state', read this instead.
attributes.//posts: Block number 3 is the two posts: wood or dressed stone, so a tower can match what it stands next to. Every alternative must resolve to at least one loaded block or MultiblockStructure.HighlightIncompleteParts throws on SearchBlocks(wildcard)[0]; RopewayModSystem.VerifyStructureWildcards logs that at startup, but it only tests the whole key, so a dud alternative hides behind the live ones. These are the vanilla 1.22.1 codes: log-placed-{wood}-{rotation}, debarkedlog-*, planks-*, rock-*, cobblestone-*, drystone-*, rockpolished-*, stonebricks-*. WildcardUtil anchors an @-pattern as ^...$ (RegexCache.IsMatch), so rock-.* does not also swallow crackedrock-*. Deliberately NOT widened to slabs, stairs, chiselled blocks or soil: a post is a structural column, and a tower that accepts anything stops reading as a tower.
attributes.//blockNumber1: A PLAIN tower wears the plain sheave, and only that. The bullwheel used to be an accepted alternative here, back when it was decoration and a drive tower was the same sixteen cells as any other; it is now the centre cell of a STATION, whose whole crossarm is a drive train, so accepting one on a plain tower would let a wheel that is joined to nothing turn on a tower that drives nothing. RopewayAssetContractTests.AStationWearsTheBullwheelAndAPlainTowerWearsTheHead is what pins the split.
attributes.//multiblockStructure: One crossarm on two posts, all offsets from the footing you place on the ground. ropeway:drivestation and ropeway:tensionstation carry this SAME offset list byte for byte and differ only in which block each cell wants, which is what keeps every clearance below valid for a station without re-deriving one of them. The crossarm is at y +4 and not lower: the cabin is 2.5 blocks tall, hangs 2.25 below the rope, and passes over this very block, so the sheave has to sit 4.5 above the footing's bottom for the floor to clear the footing and the roof to clear the station rails. The posts run the whole way down to ground level, y 0..3, or they hang in the air beside the footing. The passage cells (x -2..2, y 0..3) are deliberately absent.
attributes.//passagewidth: The posts sit at x +/-3 and the crossarm is SEVEN cells, leaving a 5-wide passage. It was 5 cells and a 3-wide passage. THIS IS THE FIX, not decoration: moving the posts out is what takes post penetration from 1.000 to 0.033 blocks at a 45-degree corner and from 0.450 to 0.000 at 30 degrees. An earlier note here said the opposite - that the widening was 'room and light' and that the angle-station yaw law was the fix. Backwards on both counts: the yaw law measured WORSE (45deg 0.033 -> 1.000, 30deg 0.000 -> 0.331), because the cabin crab-walks once PositionAt has swung its origin onto the outgoing leg, and it was reverted. Do not re-attempt it. A right-angle corner still clips whatever the yaw does - a facing is one of four cardinals, so at 90 degrees the outgoing leg IS the post axis and the cabin's origin travels through the post column, which is a translation no rotation fixes. The widening used to cost metal - brace.json yielded 4, so five wide was one craft and seven wide was two - and an earlier note here argued about that price at length. It costs nothing now: the recipe pass took the yield to 8, so six braces is one craft either way, and DECISIONS.md section 3's marginal-per-tower worry does not reach this. Do not re-narrow the passage to save metal there is none to save.
